scenario: A workflow that creates a ticket for every signed contract stops running after an app update. No errors appear anywhere.
question: How would you catch this?

options.text: Add a heartbeat check that alerts when the expected number of tickets is missing in a window, such as none created in a weekday.
Wait for the error alert, since failures always produce one.
Ask the sales team to tell you if tickets look low.

why: A silent no-run produces no error message. Only a check for the missing result can see it.

scenario: Your automation alerts post to a shared channel that most people have muted.
question: What is the better design?

options.text: Route by severity to a named owner with a backup, put the automation name, symptom and next step in the alert and test the route every quarter.
Post every alert to a bigger channel so more people see it.
Turn alerts off since nobody reads them anyway.

why: An alert nobody reads is the same as no alert. Ownership, a backup and a tested route are what make an alert work.

scenario: A run finishes with no error, but a sample check shows 46 tickets created for 50 signed contracts.
question: What does this show?

options.text: A wrong-output failure that status colors cannot see. Reconcile counts, find the four missing items and fix the cause.
The automation is healthy because the run was green.
Ignore it. Four out of fifty is close enough.

why: A run that finishes without error has not proved the result is right. Count reconciliation catches silent gaps.

scenario: You are choosing between alerting on 'step four retried twice' and alerting on 'no invoices created today'.
question: Which do you set up first?

options.text: The symptom alert, no invoices created, because it catches any cause, including ones you did not anticipate.
The step retry alert, since it shows the exact cause.
Neither. Review the dashboard when you remember.

why: Cause alerts only fire for causes you predicted. A missing result always triggers a symptom alert.

scenario: Your urgent alert channel has fired ten times in a month and was ignored all ten times.
question: What should happen?

options.text: Review it in the monthly hygiene pass: remove it, merge it with a duplicate or move it to a digest, so urgent alerts stay meaningful.
Keep it. It might matter one day.
Add more urgent alerts so nobody can miss a real one.

why: People can react urgently only a few times a day before fatigue sets in. Alerts that are routinely harmless teach people to ignore alerts.
